questions.question: Logistic regression is primarily used for:
options: Classification, despite the word regression in its name
Reducing the number of input columns
questions.explanation: For binary classification, logistic regression estimates a class probability from a weighted feature score.

questions.question: For any finite real score z, the sigmoid σ(z) maps to:
questions.explanation: The sigmoid maps a real-valued score to a value strictly between zero and one.

questions.question: Which quantity is modelled as a linear function of the features in logistic regression?
questions.explanation: The logit transform makes the log-odds a linear function of the inputs.

questions.question: If a logistic-regression coefficient is 2.0, its one-unit odds ratio is approximately:
questions.explanation: The odds ratio for a one-unit increase is exp(β); exp(2) is about 7.39, conditional on other features.

questions.question: Which loss is equivalent to negative Bernoulli log-likelihood for binary labels?
questions.explanation: Maximising the Bernoulli likelihood is equivalent to minimising its negative log-likelihood, called binary log-loss.

questions.question: A scikit-learn ConvergenceWarning during LogisticRegression most often means:
options: The solver did not converge within its iteration limit; scale features, allow more iterations, and inspect the fit
The model automatically changed the positive class
questions.explanation: A convergence warning should be investigated. Scaling within a training pipeline and increasing max_iter may help; also check data separation and collinearity rather than ignoring the warning.

questions.question: With rows as true labels and columns as predicted labels, where is a false negative for positive class 1?
questions.explanation: A false negative is a real positive example predicted as negative.

questions.question: A rare positive class matters, and missing a real positive is costly. Which metric is most directly about the fraction of actual positives found?
questions.explanation: Recall = TP/(TP + FN); when missed positives are costly, recall is important, alongside the false-positive trade-off.

questions.question: A dataset is 95% negative. A model that always predicts negative will achieve approximately:
questions.explanation: This illustrates why accuracy alone can hide failure on a rare positive class.

questions.question: If missed positives are costly, which threshold change will generally move toward higher recall, often at the cost of more false positives?
questions.explanation: Lowering the threshold generally labels more cases positive, which can raise recall and also increase false positives; choose it using validation data.
